thread.title: Nicholas Ward Positions For 2019: Cautiously Optimistic And Focused On Dividend Growth - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)

author: Nicholas Ward
title: Nicholas Ward Positions For 2019: Cautiously Optimistic And Focused On Dividend Growth - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)
text:
What do you expect to be the key driver of stock market performance in 2019? The unfortunate answer to this question is sentiment. I suspect that the volatility that we've seen emerge during 2018 is here to stay. Until we overcome some of the political and trade hurdles that are currently weighing on the broader market, causing global growth projections to become murky, I expect that the market will continue to shoot first and ask questions later with regard to selling the news. I think this makes for a trader's market in the short-term that will also likely create attractive long-term opportunities for buy-and-hold type investors who have the intestinal fortitude to deal with abnormal volatility.
As we approach 2019, are you bullish or bearish on U.S. stocks? Although sentiment is pretty negative at the moment, I remain moderately bullish. I don't think we've seen the major, high volume flush out that would typically represent a bottom. This is concerning to me and I could definitely see the market continuing to churn lower for awhile, but eventually, I expect the fundamentals to create a floor in the market. I expect to see a deceleration of earnings growth in 2019 as we come off the heels of comparisons that were bolstered by tax reform benefits; however, I still think we'll see mid-single digit earnings growth. After the current market weakness, I think we're trading near fair value when you look at the market through a wider lens. Assuming the S&P 500's bottom-line does post moderate growth, I think 2019 performance will be in-line with long-term market performance, with gains of 7-10%. If there is some sort of black swan event that causes EPS growth to net negative, then all bets are off. However, right now, I think an earnings recession is much more likely than an actual recession in 2019 and I'm allocation capital accordingly.
Which domestic/global issue is most likely to adversely affect U.S. markets in the coming year? Domestically, I'm most concerned about a constitutional crisis involving Donald Trump and the mounting legal pressures that seem to be surrounding his administration (and personal businesses). Looking back, the market didn't perform particularly well during the Watergate period. Granted, this is all very speculative, but now that the Democrats have taken over power of the House, I think the risk of the impeachment process becoming a reality has increased should the Mueller report bear negative news for the President.
On the flip side, if there is bombshell news that results in a change in the Oval Office, I could imagine a scenario where the market actually views it as a net positive if it would result in less pressure on Chinese trade. It seems clear that Wall Street is bearish on the tariffs and harsh trade rhetoric coming out of the White House and if this changes and the focus is brought back to something more productive, like infrastructure, for instance, I suspect it will be bullish for the market.
This is a good segue into the global issue that I'm most concerned about for 2019, which happens to be the same global issue that has dominated the news cycle throughout 2018: the trade war with China. The trade war that we've embarked on against China has certainly hurt the U.S. and global economy. If it is not resolved soon, I suspect this trend will only grow worse. The market never likes uncertainty and when the two largest economies in the world are feuding (and potentially slowing in response), the threat of a global slowdown becomes real.
How does the political climate affect the risks and opportunities for next year? I just touched on this, but I think political issues have the potential to create significant volatility in the markets during 2019. Typically, the third year of a first-term President is a bullish one for the market. Hopefully, that trend holds true, though I do have my concerns. I would love to see the policy makers in Washington work together and be productive for the American people, though I fear there will be more fighting between the parties. Donald Trump has ushered the U.S. into a very divisive period of time. Most of the noise coming out of D.C. is just that: noise. It's more politicking than anything else if you ask me. Politicians are constantly pandering to their bases rather than trying to compromise. Crossing the isle signifies weakness in this day and age with the majority of U.S. elected officials seemingly more loyal to their political party than their country as a whole. I don't know what will cause the pendulum to swing the other way, but in the meantime, I will do my best to ignore most of the political-based headwinds and focus on company fundamentals.
Do you expect the yield curve to continue flattening in 2019, and if so what impacts will that have on the equity market and the economy in general? The curve is already pretty flat. Will the 2's and 10's invert in 2019? I think that's a possibility. Using history as a guide, that would seem to point toward a recession in the next 16 months or so. However, during the period of time between the yield inversion and the start of a recession, the stock market typically performs well. In other words, there is no easy way to time the markets using the yield curve. Furthermore, with interest rates being manipulated globally in an unprecedented way, I'm not sure if any historical data related to the yields/inversion is relevant today. I have lightened up on banking stocks as a proactive measure against the flattening curve. However, I'm not getting out of equities because of recessionary fears.
In terms of asset allocation, how are you positioned heading into the New Year? I'm very long equities. As a dividend growth investor, holding assets like cash, gold, or bonds doesn't make much sense, since they don't generate the reliably increasing income that is the foundation of my investment strategy. In 2018 my passive income stream posted double-digit growth and right now, forward-looking income projections are pointing towards another year of double-digit dividend growth for me in 2019. This is the beauty of a dividend growth strategy. The market goes up and down and yet, my passive income, which is my primary concern, continues to compound and grow in a relatively predictable way.
I have been making trades to increase the quality of my holdings, reducing exposure to more interest rate sensitive stocks and more speculative companies. However, I'm still ~92% long equities with the other ~8% in cash. My cash exposure has hovered between 7% and 12% for the last 18 months or so. Right now I'm towards the bottom end of the range, having made several purchases in recent weeks during the market's latest sell-off. I would be happy to continue to increase my equity exposure into 2019 as high-quality DGI names are discounted.
What surprise do you see in the market that isn't currently getting sufficient investor attention? Although it's clearly speculative at this point, I think the possibility of a major infrastructure bill isn't being priced into the market. I'm not sure what the chance of such a bill would be, but heading into the 2020 campaign season, I can imagine that the GOP is going to want to get some positive news going (especially if economic fears continue to grow surrounding the current trade policies). I think some of the industrials/cyclical that would really benefit from a domestic infrastructure deal are really cheap right now and would likely generate strong, double-digit returns should infrastructure get passed by Congress.
Also, I think the market has been whistling by the graveyard, looking past our rising national debt for decades now. Austerity doesn't play well in Washington D.C. for either political party. Heck, the Republicans are supposed to be the fiscally conservative party and we've seen the budget deficit balloon under their leadership in recent years leading me to believe that all hope may be lost with regard to reducing the national debt in any significant way. Rising rates during an expanding budget deficit are fairly unprecedented and I don't know what the fallout will be. I think this is a real risk to the economy and the markets; however, I've been worried about these national balance sheet related issues for quite some time and I think they're more of a persistent worry, rather than something specifically related to 2019.
What role will the Fed play in the coming year? I think the Fed's role in 2019 market movements will be minimal. I can only assume that Powell has learned from the lesson of his more hawkish rhetoric in October and I suspect to see a dovish/data dependent Fed in 2019. So long as the Fed is dedicated towards the "data dependent" statements, I think it will slip quietly into the market background. If I'm wrong, the market could be in for some pain. Though, I have to believe that the men and women are the Fed are smart individuals and hopefully, they'll be more focused on the economic data rather than their dot plots. I do with the President would stop being a thorn in Powell's side on Twitter. The independence of the Fed is paramount to the U.S./global economic system and I think the Fed will (stubbornly) do what it has to do to maintain that. If the President wants the Fed to stop raising rates, I think the best thing he could do is keep his conversations with the Fed private. As Jeffrey Gundlach recently said, Trump is backing Powell back into a "damned if you do, damned if you don't" type situation and this isn't good for the market as a whole.
What issue is receiving too much investor attention and/or is already priced in? The sell-off in Apple ( AAPL ) shares and the rumors of that company's demise seem overly exaggerated to me. Apple remains arguably the greatest company of all time. It continues to post record cash flows and shareholder returns. I don't think we're going to see a major drop off in iPhone sales. I expect iPhone units to be relatively flat in 2019, services and wearable's to continue to grow nicely, and for the company to post substantial bottom line growth on the tails of its ~$100b buyback. Even if iPhone sales slump a bit in 2019, it's not as if this company isn't going to be profitable. If you combine this with the potential for AAPL management to reduce the outstanding share count by 5-10%, I think Apple's low multiple makes little sense. Apple is my largest holding by far and I'm very content to hold these shares headed into 2019. I expect to see another dividend increase between 8-12% in 2019 from AAPL. All in all, the Apple weakness seems irrational to me and I think investors who're bullish on these shares at the moment will be rewarded richly over the long-term.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
